kurz: Why the remaining maturity says little about a bond's interest rate risk, and how to calculate that risk with duration and convexity.

bloecke.md:
Two bonds have a term of ten years. One pays a 5% coupon, the other none at all. If interest rates rise by one percentage point, the first loses 7.6% of its market value and the second 9.2%. Remaining maturity, creditworthiness and currency are identical; the only difference is how the cash flows are distributed. The remaining maturity is therefore not suitable as a measure of interest rate risk.

The reason lies in the present value formula. Each individual payment is discounted at the market interest rate, and the further in the future it lies, the more strongly its present value reacts to a change in this rate. A bond with high coupons pays back part of the capital early, and the investor can reinvest it on the new terms. With a bond without a coupon, the entire value depends on the single payment at the end of the term. What is needed, then, is a measure of the average point in time of the cash flows instead of the end of the term.

bloecke.titel: Interest rate sensitivity by term and coupon

bloecke.md: The table is calculated using the market yield on ten-year German federal bonds on 18 September 2026, that is 3.52%. It shows two patterns. First, sensitivity rises with the term, but not proportionally. From 10 to 30 years the remaining maturity triples, while the modified duration of a 2.5% bond only grows from 8.61 to 19.69. Second, coupons lower the measure because they return part of the capital earlier.

## Macaulay duration

Frederick Macaulay introduced the measure in 1938 in a study for the National Bureau of Economic Research. To picture it, imagine each payment as a weight on a timeline. The weight is its share of the total present value; the lever arm is the time of payment. The centre of gravity of this arrangement is the duration, that is the average period for which capital is tied up, in years.

bloecke.formel: D_mac = [ Sum over t of t × CF_t / (1 + y)^t ] / P
bloecke.erklaerung: The formula gives the present-value-weighted average period for which capital is tied up, in years. For every coupon bond the result is below the remaining maturity. For a zero-coupon bond it matches the remaining maturity exactly, because there is only a single payment.

Almost four fifths of the present value is accounted for by the final payment. That is why the centre of gravity is at 8.91 years and not at the midpoint of the term at five years. The same distribution explains why the zero-coupon bond is more sensitive: for it, the share is one hundred per cent.

## Modified duration

Macaulay's figure is intuitive. For trading, however, what matters more is how much price is lost when the yield rises by one percentage point. To find this, you divide the Macaulay duration by (1 + y) and obtain the modified duration, that is the sensitivity of the price to the yield.

bloecke.erklaerung: The second equation is the bond market's rule of thumb. Δy is entered in percentage points, and the result is the percentage change in price. A modified duration of 8.61 means a price loss of around 8.6% per percentage point rise in interest rates.

bloecke.titel: Rule of thumb and present value calculation
bloecke.md:
The model bond stands at 91.53. The yield jumps from 3.52% to 4.52%.

- The rule of thumb gives -8.611 × 1 = -8.61%, that is a price of 83.65.
- The exact calculation gives a price of 84.03, that is -8.19%.

The approximation is off by 0.42 percentage points. The exactly calculated loss is smaller than the predicted one, and this deviation is systematic.

bloecke.md:
## Convexity

The rule of thumb is based on the first derivative of the price-yield function and corresponds to the tangent to the curve. A tangent touches the curve at one point and moves away from it everywhere else. Because the curve is convex, that is it sags downwards, it lies above the straight line for any deviation. For the bondholder this is consistently favourable, because the rule of thumb overestimates their losses and underestimates their gains.

This error is corrected by the second term of the Taylor series, the convexity.

bloecke.erklaerung: C is the convexity. It is calculated as the present-value-weighted sum over t × (t+1) × CF_t, divided by P × (1+y)². Here Δy is entered as a decimal; one percentage point corresponds to 0.01. Because Δy is squared, the correction term is always positive when convexity is positive, regardless of the direction in which the interest rate moves.
variablen: change in interest rate as a decimal
bloecke.beispiel: For +2 percentage points: -8.611 × 0.02 + 0.5 × 87.95 × 0.02² = -0.1722 + 0.0176 = -0.1546, that is -15.46%. The exact calculation gives -15.59%.

bloecke.titel: Price change by three methods of calculation

bloecke.md: Up to a change in interest rates of about half a percentage point, duration alone is accurate enough. Up to two points, convexity improves the result considerably; beyond that, only the full present value calculation is reliable. Because the correction is positive regardless of direction, high convexity is an advantage. For the same interest rate step, the price gain is larger and the price loss smaller. This property has a price in the market. Two bonds with identical duration but different convexity therefore do not have the same yield.

## Duration risk in 2022

In 2022, the yield on ten-year German federal bonds rose from minus 0.21% on 3 January to plus 2.53% on 30 December. That is 274 basis points in twelve months and the sharpest rise in the Bundesbank's daily series since 1997. Default risk played no part; the price losses were entirely due to duration risk.

At the start of 2022 its price was 102.12 and its yield -0.21%. Its modified duration was 10.02 and its convexity 110.5.

- For +2.74 points, the rule of thumb gives -10.02 × 2.74 = -27.5%.
- With convexity it is -27.46 + 0.5 × 110.5 × 0.0274² = -23.3%.
- At the year-end yield and an unchanged remaining maturity of ten years, the price is 77.89, that is -23.7%.

The rule of thumb was thus off by just under four percentage points. Convexity explains almost the entire deviation.

## Austria's bond with a term of one hundred years

In September 2017 the Republic of Austria issued a bond maturing on 20 September 2117. The coupon was 2.10%, the issue price 99.50 and the yield at issue 2.11%. The Macaulay duration was around 42 years, more than four times that of a typical ten-year government bond. The security had no significant default risk, but the greatest interest rate risk the European government bond market had to offer.

Three years later the yield had fallen to around 0.5%. Because duration itself depends on the level of interest rates, it had risen to almost 60 years during this phase. As the price rose, so did the interest rate sensitivity. At the end of 2020 the security was quoted at 221.66; during the year it had reached 247.64. After that, the interest rate trend reversed.

bloecke.unter: Year-end price as a percentage of face value, 2026 as of 18 September, ISIN AT0000A1XML2; from its peak of 247.64 in 2020 it had fallen to 55.09 by then, that is by 78%, with unchanged creditworthiness.

bloecke.md: In 2022 alone, the price fell from 155.00 to 73.10, that is by 52.8%. On 18 September 2026 the bond is quoted at 55.09, which corresponds to a yield to maturity of around 3.9%. Its modified duration has thus fallen to 26.4, and its convexity to around 1,300. Investors who bought at the peak price in 2020 are carrying a price loss of more than three quarters, even though there was never any doubt about the debtor's ability to pay.

At the start of 2022 this bond had a modified duration of 51.4, and its yield rose from 1.15% to 2.95% over the year. For this, the rule of thumb predicts a price loss of 92%, and with convexity 32%. The actual price loss was 52.8%.

Duration and convexity are derivatives that only apply close to one point on the curve. With a duration above 50 and an interest rate jump of almost two points, you move far away from this point; over the year, the modified duration itself fell from 51 to 33. For extremely long terms, both measures are therefore only suitable for a rough assessment; for a forecast you have to recalculate.

bloecke.titel: Price change with falling and rising interest rates
bloecke.unter: Exact present value calculation as of 18 September 2026; for every bond, the price rise when rates fall is larger than the price fall when rates rise, and this convexity effect grows with duration.

bloecke.md:
## Immunisation

Rising interest rates have two opposing effects. The price falls immediately, which is a loss. At the same time, all future coupons can be reinvested at higher rates, which is a gain. The price loss occurs early and once; the reinvestment gain occurs late and cumulatively. There is therefore a point in time at which the two effects balance out, and this point in time is the Macaulay duration. Frank Redington described the method in 1952 and called it immunisation.

bloecke.titel: Final value per €100 of face value after an immediate interest rate shock

bloecke.md: The final value in the middle column only ranges between 124.59 and 124.72, a range of a tenth of a per cent for a four percentage point movement in interest rates. To the left of it, price risk predominates; to the right, reinvestment risk. The fact that the final value in the middle never falls below the value at an unchanged yield is again due to convexity. The bondholder gains a little in both directions.

For a goal with a fixed date, such as a tax payment, a down payment or an expiring loan agreement, the duration of the bonds is matched to this date, rather than the remaining maturity. With individual bonds, coupon and maturity must be considered together, because a high coupon noticeably shortens the duration. Fixed-maturity ETFs with a set liquidation date replicate this approach. Traditional bond ETFs, by contrast, keep their duration constant and are not geared to any end date.

## Effective duration in the factsheet

For bonds with a call right, conversion right or early repayment, the analytical formula fails because the cash flows are not fixed. Instead, the **effective duration** is determined numerically. To do this, the yield curve is shifted up and down by a small amount in the calculation, the security is revalued each time, and the price reaction is measured. This figure appears in every ETF factsheet. The iShares Core U.S. Aggregate Bond ETF, one of the largest US bond ETFs, reports an effective duration of 5.75 years as of 17 September 2026, with a yield to maturity of 5.23%. A rise in interest rates of one percentage point costs around 5.75% in price there, set against just over 5% of current income.

With callable securities, convexity can become negative. If interest rates fall, the issuer calls the bond and refinances more cheaply. The price therefore hardly rises above the redemption price. If interest rates rise, the bond remains outstanding and its price falls in full. The advantage of positive convexity thus turns into a disadvantage. A conspicuously high coupon on a subordinated bank bond is often the compensation for this feature.

The rule of thumb assumes a **parallel shift** of the entire yield curve. In reality, the curve twists more often than it shifts in parallel. In 2022, for example, the two-year Bund yield rose by 325 basis points and the ten-year yield by only 274. Two portfolios with identical overall duration react very differently to this, depending on whether their duration comes from short or long securities.

In practice there are three refinements for this. **Key rate duration** measures sensitivity to a movement at a single point on the curve, for example at two, five or ten years, and leaves the rest of the curve unchanged. **Spread duration** measures the same for a widening of the risk premium instead of the base rate; for corporate bonds it is often the more important figure. **Portfolio duration** is the present-value-weighted average of the individual durations. This is possible because durations can be added up, whereas yields to maturity cannot.

An effective duration of 5.75 does not mean that something is paid out in 5.75 years. It measures price sensitivity, even though it is stated in years. A bond ETF has a duration but no repayment date. It continuously sells bonds whose remaining maturity has become too short and buys longer ones. Such a fund therefore does not promise a fixed sum on a fixed date.

mitnehmen: The remaining maturity says little about interest rate risk. What matters is the duration, that is the present-value-weighted average point in time at which the money flows back.

The percentage price change is approximately minus the modified duration times the change in interest rates in percentage points. Up to about half a percentage point, this approximation is accurate enough.
Positive convexity, as found in bonds without a call right, always corrects the rule of thumb in the bondholder's favour, because gains turn out larger and losses smaller than predicted.

The Austria 2117 bond lost over three quarters of its market value between 2020 and 2026, even though its creditworthiness was never in question. Interest rate risk and default risk must therefore be considered separately.
If the investment horizon is matched to the Macaulay duration, price risk and reinvestment risk cancel each other out. This immunisation works very precisely.

begriffe.text: Present-value-weighted average point in time of all payments of a bond, measured in years. It is also the investment horizon at which price risk and reinvestment risk cancel each other out.
Macaulay duration divided by (1 + yield). It indicates approximately by what percentage the price falls when the market yield rises by one percentage point.

Curvature of the price-yield curve and second term of the Taylor approximation. If it is positive, as with bonds without a call right, it works in the bondholder's favour whether interest rates rise or fall, and therefore has a price in the market.
Interest rate sensitivity determined numerically from simulated interest rate shocks. It is needed for securities with call or conversion rights and is a standard figure in ETF factsheets.
Matching the duration of a bond holding to the date of a future payment obligation, so that interest rate changes leave the final value practically unchanged.
